title: IV. Rebellion
paragraphs: “I have to make one confession,” Ivan began. “I could never understand how anyone can love their neighbors. It's precisely one's neighbors, to my mind, that one can't love — though one might love those at a distance. I once read somewhere of John the Merciful, a saint, that when a hungry, freezing beggar came to him, he took him into his bed, held him in his arms, and began breathing into his mouth, which was putrid and loathsome from some terrible disease. I'm convinced he did that out of ‘self-laceration,’ out of the self-laceration of falsity, for the sake of the charity imposed by duty, as a penance laid on him. For anyone to love a man, the man has to be hidden — because the moment he shows his face, love is gone.”

“Father Zossima has talked about that more than once,” Alyosha observed. “He, too, said that a man's face often prevents many people — people not practiced in love — from loving him. But still, there's a great deal of love in humanity, almost Christ-like love. I know that myself, Ivan.”

“Well, I know nothing of it so far, and I can't understand it, and the countless mass of humanity is with me on that. The question is whether it's due to men's bad qualities or whether it's inherent in their nature. To my mind, Christ-like love for men is a miracle impossible on earth. He was God. But we are not gods. Suppose I, for instance, am suffering intensely. Another person can never know how much I suffer, because he is another and not I. And what's more, a man is rarely ready to admit another's suffering (as if it were some kind of distinction). Why won't he admit it, do you think? Because I smell unpleasant, because I have a stupid face, because I once stepped on his foot. Besides, there is suffering and suffering; degrading, humiliating suffering that humbles me — hunger, for instance — my benefactor will perhaps tolerate; but when you come to higher suffering — for an idea, for instance — he'll very rarely admit it, perhaps because my face strikes him as not at all what he imagines a man suffering for an idea ought to look like. And so he instantly withdraws his favor, and not at all from any badness of heart. Beggars, especially genteel beggars, should never show themselves; they should ask for charity through the newspapers instead. One can love one's neighbors in the abstract, or even at a distance, but up close it's almost impossible. If it were like on the stage, in the ballet, where beggars come in wearing silken rags and tattered lace and beg for alms dancing gracefully, then one might enjoy looking at them. But even then we wouldn't love them. But enough of that. I simply wanted to show you my point of view. I meant to speak of the suffering of humanity in general, but we'd better confine ourselves to the sufferings of the children. That reduces the scope of my argument to a tenth of what it would be. Still, we'd better stick to the children, even if it weakens my case. But, in the first place, children can be loved even at close quarters, even when they're dirty, even when they're ugly (though I think children are never ugly). The second reason I won't talk about grown-up people is that, besides being disgusting and unworthy of love, they have a compensation — they've eaten the apple and know good and evil, and they've become ‘like gods.’ They go on eating it still. But children haven't eaten anything, and they are so far innocent. Are you fond of children, Alyosha? I know you are, and you'll understand why I prefer to speak of them. If they, too, suffer horribly on earth, it must be for their fathers' sins, they must be punished for their fathers, who have eaten the apple; but that reasoning belongs to another world and is incomprehensible for the human heart here on earth. The innocent must not suffer for another's sins — and especially such innocents! You may be surprised at me, Alyosha, but I'm awfully fond of children, too. And notice — cruel people, the violent, the rapacious, the Karamazovs, are sometimes very fond of children. Children, while they're still quite small — up to seven, for instance — are so remote from grown-up people; they are, as it were, different creatures, of a different species. I knew a criminal in prison who, in the course of his career as a burglar, had murdered whole families, including several children. But in prison he developed a strange affection for them. He'd spend all his time at his window watching the children playing in the prison yard. He trained one little boy to come up to his window and became great friends with him.... You don't know why I'm telling you all this, Alyosha? My head aches and I'm sad.”
“You speak with a strange air,” Alyosha observed uneasily, “as though you weren't quite yourself.”

“By the way, a Bulgarian I met recently in Moscow,” Ivan went on, seeming not to hear his brother's words, “told me about the crimes committed by Turks and Circassians all over Bulgaria out of fear of a general Slavic uprising. They burn villages, murder, rape women and children, they nail their prisoners by the ears to the fences, leave them that way until morning, and in the morning hang them — all kinds of things you can't imagine. People sometimes speak of bestial cruelty, but that's a great injustice and an insult to the beasts; a beast can never be so cruel as a man, so artistically cruel. The tiger only tears and gnaws — that's all he can do. He'd never think of nailing people by the ears, even if he could. These Turks also took pleasure in torturing children — cutting the unborn child from its mother's womb, tossing babies into the air and catching them on the points of their bayonets before their mothers' eyes. Doing it in front of the mothers was what gave the amusement its zest. Here's another scene I found very interesting. Imagine a trembling mother with her baby in her arms, surrounded by a circle of invading Turks. They've planned a little diversion: they pet the baby, laugh to make it laugh. They succeed; the baby laughs. At that moment a Turk points a pistol four inches from the baby's face. The baby laughs with delight, holds out its little hands to the pistol, and he pulls the trigger in the baby's face and blows out its brains. Artistic, wasn't it? By the way, Turks are particularly fond of sweet things, they say.”
“Brother, what are you driving at?” Alyosha asked.
“I think that if the devil doesn't exist but man has created him, then he has created him in his own image and likeness.”
“Just as he did God, then?” Alyosha observed.

“‘It's wonderful how you can turn words,’ as Polonius says in _Hamlet_,” Ivan laughed. “You turn my words against me. Well, I'm glad. Yours must be a fine God, if man created Him in his image and likeness. You asked just now what I was driving at. You see, I'm fond of collecting certain facts, and would you believe, I even copy down anecdotes of a certain kind from newspapers and books, and I already have a fine collection. The Turks, naturally, have made it in, but they're foreigners. I have specimens from home that are even better than the Turks. You know we prefer beating — rods and scourges — that's our national institution. Nailing ears is unthinkable for us, because after all, we're Europeans. But the rod and the scourge are always with us and they cannot be taken from us. Abroad now they hardly do any beating at all. Manners are more humane, or laws have been passed, so they don't dare to flog men anymore. But they make up for it in another way, just as national as ours is. And so national that it would be practically impossible among us — though I believe we're being inoculated with it, ever since the religious movement began in our aristocracy. I have a charming pamphlet, translated from the French, describing how, quite recently, five years ago, a murderer named Richard was executed — a young man, I believe, of twenty-three, who repented and was converted to the Christian faith on the very scaffold. This Richard was an illegitimate child who was given away by his parents at the age of six to some shepherds in the Swiss mountains. They brought him up to work for them. He grew up like a little wild beast among them. The shepherds taught him nothing and hardly fed or clothed him, but sent him out at seven to herd the flock in cold and wet, and none of them hesitated or scrupled to treat him that way. Quite the contrary, they thought they had every right, because Richard had been given to them as a piece of property, and they didn't even see the need to feed him. Richard himself describes how in those years, like the Prodigal Son in the Gospel, he longed to eat the mash given to the pigs, which were being fattened for sale. But they wouldn't even give him that, and beat him when he stole from the pigs. And that was how he spent his whole childhood and youth, until he grew up and was strong enough to run away and become a thief. The savage began to earn his living as a day laborer in Geneva. He drank what he earned, he lived like a brute, and finally killed and robbed an old man. He was caught, tried, and condemned to death. They're not sentimentalists there. And in prison he was immediately surrounded by pastors, members of Christian brotherhoods, philanthropic ladies, and the like. They taught him to read and write in prison and expounded the Gospel to him. They exhorted him, worked on him, drummed at him incessantly, until at last he solemnly confessed his crime. He was converted. He wrote to the court himself that he was a monster, but that in the end God had granted him light and shown him grace. All of Geneva was in an uproar over him — all of philanthropic and religious Geneva. All the aristocratic and well-bred society of the town rushed to the prison, kissed Richard and embraced him: ‘You are our brother, you have found grace.’ And Richard does nothing but weep with emotion: ‘Yes, I've found grace! All my youth and childhood I was glad of pigs' food, but now even I have found grace. I'm dying in the Lord.’ ‘Yes, Richard, die in the Lord; you have shed blood and must die. Though it's not your fault that you didn't know the Lord when you coveted the pigs' food and were beaten for stealing it (which was very wrong of you, because stealing is forbidden) — but you've shed blood and you must die.’ And on the last day, Richard, perfectly limp, does nothing but cry and repeat every minute: ‘This is my happiest day. I am going to the Lord.’ ‘Yes,’ cry the pastors and the judges and philanthropic ladies. ‘This is the happiest day of your life, because you're going to the Lord!’ They all walk or drive to the scaffold in procession behind the prison van. At the scaffold they call out to Richard: ‘Die, brother, die in the Lord, for even you have found grace!’ And so, covered with his brothers' kisses, Richard is dragged to the scaffold and led to the guillotine. And they chopped off his head in brotherly fashion, because he had found grace. Yes, that's characteristic. That pamphlet has been translated into Russian by some Russian philanthropists of aristocratic rank and evangelical aspirations, and distributed free of charge for the enlightenment of the common people. The case of Richard is interesting because it's national. Though it's absurd to us to chop off a man's head because he's become our brother and found grace, we have our own specialty, which is almost worse. Our historical pastime is the direct satisfaction of inflicting pain. There are lines in Nekrasov describing how a peasant lashes a horse on the eyes, ‘on its meek eyes’ — everyone must have seen it. It's peculiarly Russian. He describes how a feeble little nag has collapsed under too heavy a load and can't move. The peasant beats it, beats it savagely, at last beating it without even knowing what he's doing in the intoxication of cruelty, thrashing it mercilessly over and over. ‘However weak you are, you must pull, even if it kills you.’ The nag strains, and then he starts lashing the poor defenseless creature on its weeping, on its ‘meek eyes.’ The frantic beast tugs and drags the load, trembling all over, gasping for breath, moving sideways, with a sort of unnatural spasmodic action — it's horrible in Nekrasov. But that's only a horse, and God gave horses to be beaten. So the Tatars taught us, and they left us the knout as a remembrance of it. But men, too, can be beaten. A well-educated, cultured gentleman and his wife beat their own child with a birch rod — a little girl of seven. I have an exact account of it. The papa was glad that the birch was covered with twigs. ‘It stings more,’ he said, and so he began stinging his daughter. I know for a fact that there are people who get worked up with every blow, worked up to sensuality, to literal sensuality that increases progressively with each blow they inflict. They beat for a minute, for five minutes, for ten minutes, more and more often, more and more savagely. The child screams. At last the child can't even scream, it just gasps, ‘Daddy! daddy!’ By some diabolical, grotesque chance the case was brought into court. A lawyer was engaged. The Russian people have long called a barrister ‘a conscience for hire.’ The counsel protests in defense of his client. ‘It's such a simple thing,’ he says, ‘an everyday domestic event. A father corrects his child. To our shame be it said, it has been brought into court.’ The jury, convinced by him, returns a favorable verdict. The public roars with delight that the torturer has been acquitted. Ah, what a pity I wasn't there! I'd have proposed raising a subscription in his honor! Charming little pictures.

“But I have still better things about children. I've collected a great, great deal about Russian children, Alyosha. There was a little girl of five who was hated by her father and mother, ‘most worthy and respectable people, of good education and breeding.’ You see, I must say it again: in many people there is this peculiar trait, this love of torturing children, and children only. Toward every other kind of person these torturers behave mildly and benevolently, like cultivated and humane Europeans; but they're very fond of tormenting children — even fond of children themselves in that sense. It's the very defenselessness of the child that tempts the tormentor, the very angelic trust of the child who has no refuge and no one to appeal to, that sets his vile blood on fire. In every man, of course, a demon lies hidden — the demon of rage, the demon of lustful heat at the screams of the tortured victim, the demon of lawlessness let off its chain, the demon of the diseases that follow vice, gout, kidney disease, and so on.

“This poor child of five was subjected to every possible torture by those cultivated parents. They beat her, thrashed her, kicked her for no reason until her body was one bruise. Then they refined their cruelty further — they shut her up all night in the cold and frost in a privy, and because she didn't ask to be let out in the night (as if a child of five, sleeping its angelic, sound sleep, could be trained to wake up and ask), they smeared her face and filled her mouth with excrement — and it was her mother, her own mother, who did it. And that mother could sleep, hearing the poor child's groans! Can you understand why a little creature, who can't even understand what's being done to her, should beat her little aching heart with her tiny fist in the dark and the cold, and weep her meek, unresentful tears to dear, kind God to protect her? Do you understand that, my friend and brother, you pious and humble novice? Do you understand why this infamy must exist and is permitted? Without it, I'm told, man could not have existed on earth, because he could not have known good and evil. Why should he know that diabolical good and evil when it costs so much? Why, the whole world of knowledge is not worth that child's prayer to ‘dear, kind God’! I say nothing of the sufferings of grown-up people — they've eaten the apple, damn them, and the devil take them all! But these little ones! I'm making you suffer, Alyosha, you aren't yourself. I'll stop, if you like.”
“Never mind. I want to suffer too,” Alyosha muttered.

“One picture, just one more, because it's so curious, so characteristic, and I only just read it in some collection of Russian antiquities. I've forgotten the name — I must look it up. It was in the darkest days of serfdom, at the beginning of the century, and long live the Liberator of the People! There was in those days a general of aristocratic connections, the owner of great estates, one of those men — somewhat exceptional, I believe, even then — who, retiring from the service into a life of leisure, are convinced they've earned absolute power over the lives of their subjects. There were such men then. So our general, settled on his property of two thousand souls, lives in pomp and domineers over his poor neighbors as though they were his dependents and buffoons. He has kennels of hundreds of hounds and nearly a hundred dog-boys — all mounted and in uniform. One day a serf boy, a little child of eight, threw a stone in play and hurt the paw of the general's favorite hound. ‘Why is my favorite dog lame?’ He is told that the boy threw a stone that injured the dog's paw. ‘So you did it.’ The general looked the child up and down. ‘Take him.’ He was taken — taken from his mother and kept shut up all night. Early the next morning the general rides out with the hounds, his dependents, dog-boys, and huntsmen, all mounted around him in full hunting parade. The servants are summoned for their edification, and in front of them all stands the mother of the child. The child is brought from the lock-up. It's a gloomy, cold, foggy autumn day — a perfect day for hunting. The general orders the child to be undressed; the child is stripped naked. He shivers, numb with terror, not daring to cry.... ‘Make him run,’ the general commands. ‘Run! run!’ shout the dog-boys. The boy runs.... ‘At him!’ yells the general, and he sets the whole pack of hounds on the child. The hounds catch him and tear him to pieces before his mother's eyes!... I believe the general was afterward declared incapable of administering his estates. Well — what did he deserve? To be shot? To be shot for the satisfaction of our moral feelings? Speak, Alyosha!”
“To be shot,” Alyosha murmured, lifting his eyes to Ivan with a pale, twisted smile.
“Bravo!” Ivan cried, delighted. “If even you say so.... You're a fine monk! So there's a little devil sitting in your heart, Alyosha Karamazov!”
“What I said was absurd, but —”

“That's just the point — that ‘but’!” Ivan cried. “Let me tell you, novice, that the absurd is only too necessary on earth. The world stands on absurdities, and perhaps nothing would ever have come to pass in it without them. We know what we know!”
“What do you know?”

“I understand nothing,” Ivan went on, as if in a delirium. “I don't want to understand anything now. I want to stick to the fact. I made up my mind long ago not to understand. If I try to understand anything, I'll be unfaithful to the fact, and I've determined to stick to the fact.”
“Why are you testing me?” Alyosha cried with sudden distress. “Will you say what you mean at last?”
“Of course I will; that's what I've been leading up to. You are dear to me — I don't want to let you go, and I won't give you up to your Zossima.”
Ivan fell silent for a moment, and his face suddenly became very sad.

“Listen! I took the case of children only to make my case clearer. Of the other tears of humanity with which the earth is soaked from its crust to its center, I'll say nothing. I've narrowed my subject on purpose. I am a bug, and I recognize in all humility that I can't understand why the world is arranged as it is. Men are themselves to blame, I suppose; they were given paradise, they wanted freedom, and they stole fire from heaven, though they knew they would become unhappy — so there's no need to pity them. With my pitiful, earthly, Euclidian understanding, all I know is that there is suffering and that there is no one guilty; that cause follows effect, simply and directly; that everything flows and finds its level — but that's only Euclidian nonsense, I know, and I can't consent to live by it! What comfort is it to me that no one is guilty and that cause follows effect simply and directly, and that I know it? I must have justice, or I'll destroy myself. And not justice in some remote, infinite time and space — but here on earth, and that I could see for myself. I've believed in it. I want to see it, and if I'm dead by then, let me rise again, because if it all happens without me, it will be too unfair. Surely I haven't suffered simply so that I, my crimes and my sufferings, may manure the soil of future harmony for somebody else. I want to see with my own eyes the hind lie down with the lion, and the victim rise up and embrace his murderer. I want to be there when everyone suddenly understands what it was all for. All the religions of the world are built on this longing, and I am a believer. But then there are the children — and what am I to do about them? That's a question I can't answer. For the hundredth time I repeat, there are countless questions, but I've only taken the children, because in their case what I mean is so unanswerably clear. Listen! If all must suffer to pay for the eternal harmony, what have the children to do with it, tell me, please? It's beyond all comprehension why they should have to suffer, and why they should pay for the harmony. Why should they, too, furnish material to enrich the soil for the harmony of the future? I understand solidarity in sin among men. I understand solidarity in retribution, too; but there can be no such solidarity with children. And if it's really true that they must share responsibility for all their fathers' crimes, then such a truth is not of this world and is beyond my comprehension. Some jester will say, perhaps, that the child would have grown up and sinned — but you see, he didn't grow up; he was torn to pieces by the dogs at eight years old. Oh, Alyosha, I'm not blaspheming! Of course I understand what an upheaval of the universe it will be when everything in heaven and earth blends in one hymn of praise, and everything that lives and has lived cries aloud: ‘Thou art just, O Lord, for Thy ways are revealed.’ When the mother embraces the fiend who threw her child to the dogs, and all three cry aloud through their tears, ‘Thou art just, O Lord!’ then, of course, the crown of knowledge will be reached and all will be made clear. But here's what pulls me up short: I can't accept that harmony. And while I'm still on earth, I make haste to take my own measures. You see, Alyosha, perhaps it really may happen that if I live to that moment, or rise again to see it, I, too, may cry aloud with the rest, looking at the mother embracing the child's torturer, ‘Thou art just, O Lord!’ — but I don't want to cry that aloud then. While there's still time, I hurry to protect myself, and so I renounce the higher harmony altogether. It isn't worth the tears of that one tortured child who beat itself on the breast with its little fist and prayed in its stinking outhouse, with its unexpiated tears, to ‘dear, kind God’! It isn't worth it, because those tears are unatoned for. They must be atoned for, or there can be no harmony. But how? How are you going to atone for them? Is it possible? By their being avenged? But what do I care for avenging them? What do I care for a hell for oppressors? What good can hell do, when those children have already been tortured? And what becomes of harmony, if there is a hell? I want to forgive. I want to embrace. I don't want any more suffering. And if the sufferings of children go to swell the sum of sufferings that was needed to pay for truth, then I declare in advance that the truth is not worth such a price. I don't want the mother to embrace the oppressor who threw her son to the dogs! She has no right to forgive him! Let her forgive him for herself, if she wants; let her forgive the torturer for the immeasurable suffering of her mother's heart. But she has no right to forgive her tortured child's sufferings; she dare not forgive the torturer, even if the child itself were to forgive him! And if that's so, if they dare not forgive, what becomes of harmony? Is there in the whole world a being who would have the right to forgive and could forgive? I don't want harmony. Out of love for humanity, I don't want it. I would rather be left with unavenged suffering. I would rather remain with my unavenged suffering and unsatisfied indignation, _even if I'm wrong_. Besides, too high a price is being asked for harmony; it's beyond our means to pay so much to enter into it. And so I hasten to give back my entrance ticket, and if I'm an honest man I'm bound to give it back as soon as possible. And that is what I'm doing. It isn't God I don't accept, Alyosha — only I most respectfully return Him the ticket.”
“That's rebellion,” Alyosha murmured, looking down.

“Rebellion? I'm sorry you call it that,” Ivan said earnestly. “One can hardly live in rebellion, and I want to live. Tell me yourself, I challenge you — answer: imagine that you are creating the fabric of human destiny with the aim of making men happy in the end, of giving them peace and rest at last, but that it was essential and inevitable to torture to death only one tiny creature — that very baby beating its breast with its fist, for instance — and to found that edifice on its unavenged tears — would you consent to be the architect on those conditions? Tell me, and tell the truth.”
“No, I wouldn't consent,” Alyosha said softly.

“And can you admit the idea that the men for whom you are building it would agree to accept their happiness on the foundation of the unexpiated blood of a little victim? And that accepting it, they would remain happy forever?”

“No, I can't admit it. Brother,” Alyosha said suddenly, his eyes flashing, “you said just now — is there a being in the whole world who would have the right to forgive and could forgive? But there is a Being, and He can forgive everything, all and for all, because He gave His innocent blood for all and for everything. You've forgotten Him, and on Him is built the edifice, and it is to Him they cry aloud, ‘Thou art just, O Lord, for Thy ways are revealed!’”

“Ah! the One without sin and His blood! No, I haven't forgotten Him; on the contrary, I've been wondering all this time why it took you so long to bring Him in, because usually every argument on your side puts Him in the foreground. Do you know, Alyosha — don't laugh! — I made up a poem about a year ago. If you can waste another ten minutes on me, I'll tell it to you.”
“You wrote a poem?”

“Oh, no, I didn't write it,” Ivan laughed, “and I've never written two lines of poetry in my life. But I made this poem up in prose and I remembered it. I was carried away when I made it up. You'll be my first reader — that is, listener. Why should an author forgo even one listener?” Ivan smiled. “Shall I tell it to you?”
“I'm all attention,” said Alyosha.
“My poem is called ‘The Grand Inquisitor’; it's a ridiculous thing, but I want to tell it to you.”
